title: Welcome to the Institution Age: A Narrative of Change and the CTL
text_snippet: Welcome to the Institution Age: A Narrative of Change and the CTL This article introduces and defines the term Institution Age, arguing that Centers for Teaching and Learning, while long-predicted to play a central role in institutional change, no longer have the luxury of deciding whether they will play such a role following the pandemic, and in order to help their institutions respond to the ongoing disruptions and challenges in higher education in the 21st century. Narrative reflection of one director’s experience moving from former “ages” within educational development to the “Institutional Age” recounts the effects following changes to the roles of a faculty-qua-director and other staff members, as well as changes to audiences served and projects undertaken outside of the traditional scope of educational and instructional development. The pairing of narrative reflection and this account of a CTL in the Institution Age is purposeful in order to document and highlight both the material and emotional effects of the ongoing difficulties facing higher education.

title: ReSysting toward Transformative Connections: Envisioning a Relationship-Systems Pedagogy
text_snippet: ReSysting toward Transformative Connections: Envisioning a Relationship-Systems Pedagogy Inspired by the complexity of ecosystems, we envisioned Relationship Systems (ReSyst) Pedagogy as a transdisciplinary approach that fosters meaningful learning by engaging one’s positionality within the web of self, cultures, and structures. ReSyst extends and complicates the interpersonal focus implied in current relationship-rich education scholarship. This article reports on processes of training Graduate Teaching Assistants (GTAs) in ReSyst Pedagogy and the transferable lessons for faculty and GTA development. The authors share personal experiences and reflections on “teaching” relationship-centering practices. Our ongoing analysis provides a tentative persona-driven framework describing how one grows into ReSyst Pedagogy.

title: Towards Inclusive Excellence: Building an Anti-racist, Equity-oriented Community of Practice for STEM Faculty
text_snippet: Towards Inclusive Excellence: Building an Anti-racist, Equity-oriented Community of Practice for STEM Faculty The authors offer a case study description, curriculum, and analysis of a two year-long anti-racist, equity-oriented communities of practice (CoPs) for STEM faculty who teach and mentor STEM students. The CoPs aimed to grow STEM faculty capacity to disrupt systemic inequities and support historically underrepresented students. The CoPs were one facet of a larger multi-pronged program in partnership with a Tribal college and two public Hispanic-serving Institutions. The authors describe the development of the CoP curriculum, along with the evaluation, impact, and insights after two years, offering an analysis of the transformational possibilities of faculty communities of practice. Over two cohorts, the CoP trained 29 faculty from across STEM disciplines. Key results demonstrated that faculty increased the knowledge and understanding of barriers to student success, and how to use their roles to increase equity throughout their spheres of influence. In addition, faculty created communities by which to improve the reach and scope of their work. This provides a model for other institutions to build anti-racist and equity-oriented training and communities.

title: Expanding Access to and Enriching Experiences of High-Impact Practices: The Promise of Embracing a Partnership Mindset
text_snippet: Expanding Access to and Enriching Experiences of High-Impact Practices: The Promise of Embracing a Partnership Mindset Amidst debate about the value of a college degree, there remains evidence that college graduates experience personal and intellectual growth and career preparation, especially if they have the opportunity to engage in high-impact practices (HIPs). However, HIPs often remain inaccessible or inequitably implemented for many underserved student populations. We argue that embracing a partnership mindset in the development and implementation of HIPs can expand access to and enrich higher education experiences, thereby helping higher education move toward equity. title: AI professional development that centers faculty expertise
text_snippet: AI professional development that centers faculty expertise This article provides reflection on and analysis of a faculty-centered professional development series about generative AI at asmall university. Although this series of workshops could be implemented across a range of institutions, this model for faculty development would be especially valuable for low resource environments and/or institutions without a dedicated center for teaching and learning. Through informal networks and word of mouth, sessions tapped into existing expertise amongst faculty members. This kind of flexible, faculty-centered workshop has the potential to create faculty buy-in and enable faculty to be change agents to tackle these complex pedagogical challenges.

title: “[A] little bit of this, a little bit of that”: Faculty-centric approaches to implementing wellbeing strategies in the classroom
text_snippet: “[A] little bit of this, a little bit of that”: Faculty-centric approaches to implementing wellbeing strategies in the classroom This study investigates faculty attitudes towards wellbeing interventions for the classroom and their willingness to integrate wellbeing strategies into their teaching practices. Our research focuses on faculty development efforts at a large, R1 institution using Martin Seligman’s PERMA model for wellbeing. Using thematic analysis methodology, data from non-tenure track and tenured faculty were examined to identify patterns and themes related to the operationalization of PERMA. Three primary themes emerged from the data: (1) “PERMA-fying” for intentional growth and cultural integration; (2) Operationalizing the natural; (3) Difficulty connecting through time and space. The findings suggest that while there is an overall positive attitude towards PERMA-oriented strategies among faculty members, obstacles remain that stymie their full implementation. The study concludes that further research should expand beyond a single department to include diverse disciplines and appointment types to comprehensively understand faculty perspectives on wellbeing initiatives.

title: Navigating Change: Using Needs Assessment to Enhance Programming in Centers for Teaching and Learning
text_snippet: Navigating Change: Using Needs Assessment to Enhance Programming in Centers for Teaching and Learning This study explores how Centers for Teaching and Learning (CTLs) can adjust their programming and services to address evolving faculty needs in a post-pandemic context. To illustrate this, we provide an example of a comprehensive needs assessment, drawing on results from a survey and focus groups conducted at a mid-sized private university in the southwestern United States. The findings highlight key factors influencing faculty engagement and perceptions of professional learning opportunities. While faculty valued the CTL’s efforts, they identified barriers to participation such as limited time, relevance of offerings, and institutional policies. Faculty recommended enhanced communication, more targeted programming, and increased responsiveness to evolving teaching demands. These findings underscore the importance of ongoing needs assessment in fostering adaptability and strengthening faculty relationships. By prioritizing these assessments, CTLs can navigate change more effectively and better support teaching and learning in a rapidly evolving educational landscape, maintaining their relevance in promoting teaching excellence in higher education settings.

title: Faculty Writers as Learners: How Assessment Can Enrich Outcomes, Build Community, and Demonstrate the Value of Faculty Writing Programs
text_snippet: Faculty Writers as Learners: How Assessment Can Enrich Outcomes, Build Community, and Demonstrate the Value of Faculty Writing Programs As support for faculty writers becomes increasingly mainstream in higher education, institutions have expanded offerings such as writing retreats, writing groups, and coaching. While such programs have demonstrated benefits—including increased scholarly output, community building, and faculty well-being—assessments often rely on metrics such as satisfaction surveys and publication counts. This study argues for a shift toward a learning-centered approach to assess faculty writing programs. Drawing on Donald Kirkpatrick’s four-stage model of learning, it explores how writing support can contribute to deeper, long-term faculty learning and development. By centering the experiences of faculty writers and examining how they learn through writing support, this approach provides a robust way to enrich program outcomes, build community, and demonstrate programmatic value to academic leaders and institutional audiences.

title: UDL Takes a Village: University Faculty Reflections on Accountability and Infrastructure
text_snippet: UDL Takes a Village: University Faculty Reflections on Accountability and Infrastructure Over the past few decades, higher education has experienced significant transformations driven by changes in demographics, technology, academic resources, and societal expectations. Globally, universities are recognizing a responsibility to support diverse student populations through frameworks of universal access and design. As universities broaden access, welcoming the full diversity of students, growing numbers of students identifying as disabled and/or neurodivergent, first-generation students, and students from a vast array of cultural backgrounds are entering higher education. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is a framework designed to achieve inclusivity in education. The present study explores the experiences of faculty coming together to engage in UDL implementation through the research question: How do faculty reflect on their actions after a yearlong professional development training on UDL implementation? title: Understanding queer faculty of color’s time and values
text_snippet: Understanding queer faculty of color’s time and values Literature in higher education highlights how queer faculty of color are overworked and culturally taxed in the academy. Queer faculty of color often are tasked with using their time in ways that do not always benefit them professionally, thereby leaving them more likely to leave their institution. Using the College + University Teaching Environment framework, this study uses a large-scale, multi-institution quantitative dataset to explore how queer faculty of color spend their time in the academy as well as how time spent relates to personal and institutional values. Results show that queer faculty of color regardless of tenure status spend much of their time with tenure-related activities (i.e., teaching, research, service). Additionally, queer faculty of color not on the tenure track engaged more in external professional activities compared to their tenured/tenure-track counterparts. Results also revealed that alignment between time spent on various activities and personal values differed significantly based on tenure status, highlighting structural differences in queer faculty of color’s experiences.

title: From inquiry to insight: Cultivating local conversations on GenAI
text_snippet: From inquiry to insight: Cultivating local conversations on GenAI Emerging literature on faculty and student uses of generative AI (GenAI) tools shows that institutional factors like levels of adoption, demographics of students and faculty, institutional type, and institutional culture around GenAI can significantly impact perceptions and behaviors. This article argues that educational developers should collect local data to enhance their understanding of institutional behaviors and perceptions of GenAI in addition to reading national research. Aside from sharing data from a survey distributed to students (n=504) and faculty (n=281) across three campuses (two residential and one online) of a STEM-focused private university, this article explains how data informed CTL and professional training related to GenAI. Overall, this article models a replicable, locally tailored, and data-driven approach to GenAI professional development and adds to existing knowledge of student and faculty perceptions and use of GenAI tools.

title: Return to Remote: Are Higher Education Instructors Prepared for the Future in a Post-COVID World?
text_snippet: Return to Remote: Are Higher Education Instructors Prepared for the Future in a Post-COVID World? This article discusses the current 2024 “return to remote” action that has been occurring on higher education campuses. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, research has shown that there were significant gaps in higher education's emergency remote teaching (ERT) preparedness. Despite adaptations during and after the pandemic, there are still questions about whether higher education instructors are prepared for the future in a post-COVID world. This article examines current ERT readiness as well as future needs of higher education institutions. In comparing the current situation with the ERT switch that occurred in 2020, the researchers discuss issues such as faculty training and professional development, pedagogical shifts, and institutional policies. The authors call for enhanced training and professional development needs, a paradigm shift in teaching methodologies, and institutional support and policies to ensure educational continuity in future crises.

title: Interdisciplinarity and Peer Evaluation as Tools for Enhancing Graduate Student Teaching Training
text_snippet: Interdisciplinarity and Peer Evaluation as Tools for Enhancing Graduate Student Teaching Training Graduate student instructors (GSIs) play a critical role in higher education, serving as instructors of record for a substantial portion of courses at research universities. This study evaluates the structure and processes of Duke University Graduate School’s Teaching Triangles (TT) program, an interdisciplinary peer observation and feedback process designed to prepare graduate students for academic careers. Guided by the framework of communities of practice (CoP), this study explores how TT fosters pedagogical development, interdisciplinary learning, and professional preparation for GSIs. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the study analyzes 694 reflections from GSIs who participated in TT between Fall 2011 and Summer 2022. The findings indicate that TT effectively fosters a supportive environment for GSIs, promoting pedagogical self-reflection, confidence growth, and the adoption of improved teaching practices. Female GSIs, in particular, reported notable confidence gains, aligning with existing literature on gender and teaching self-efficacy. GSIs also valued the interdisciplinary nature of the program, which broadened their perspectives on teaching across various disciplines.

title: Roads to change: Exploring the lived experiences of be(com)ing among faculty who participated in educational development
text_snippet: Roads to change: Exploring the lived experiences of be(com)ing among faculty who participated in educational development The purpose of this study was to understand the lived experiences of be(com)ing among faculty members who participated in educational development. It aims to contribute to our knowledge on be(com)ing, a portmanteau of becoming and being that emphasizes that these two processes are often interconnected. I generated data for this study using semi-structured interviews with eight faculty members who participated in at least one program through the Center for Teaching and Learning at a research university in the southeastern United States. Using interpretative phenomenological analysis, I identified five themes in the data: (1) Reimagining Faculty Identities in the Academy, (2) Embracing a Culture of Experimentation, (3) Thriving Amid Constraints, (4), Building Transformative Communities, and (5) Cultivating Spaces for Equity and Inclusion. The findings of this study not only shed light on the complex landscapes that faculty members navigate but also demonstrate the potentialities of educational development to enable them to shape their professional growth in meaningful ways.

title: Social Learning Spaces and the Systems Convening Mindset: Implications for Faculty Development Professionals
text_snippet: Social Learning Spaces and the Systems Convening Mindset: Implications for Faculty Development Professionals Systems convening is a style of leadership developed by Wenger-Trayner and Wenger-Trayner (2021) that focuses on crossing social and institutional boundaries to facilitate change. Faculty developers are increasingly called on to cross disciplinary and institutional boundaries in their work supporting teaching and learning. A systems convening mindset includes being able to bring people together across boundaries, wanting to make a difference in educational outcomes, knowing the academic landscape, knowing the people to talk to in each silo, and valuing learning as a part of this leadership style (Wenger-Trayner and Wenger-Trayner, 2021). In a case study of 18 faculty developers at a multi-campus research university, we document the developers' approach to their work and evaluate the usefulness of the systems convening mindset in the context of university faculty development. We conclude that approaching faculty development leadership from a systems convening perspective can help developers successfully cultivate the cross-boundary relationships necessary to facilitate communities of change in universities.

title: Enhancing Inclusive Teaching Measurement: The Development of the Power-Sharing Practices Checklist
text_snippet: Enhancing Inclusive Teaching Measurement: The Development of the Power-Sharing Practices Checklist Inclusive teaching has become one of the most frequently written about topics in the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning and Educational Development. However, the field’s advancement is limited by an overreliance on faculty perspectives, affective student measurement, and a lack of measurement tools for specific instructor behaviors that promote inclusion. The present study took a multi-step, mixed-methods approach to the initial development of a power-sharing practices checklist. The authors created the initial items based on the examination of the literature and focus groups with both faculty and students. The checklist was administered to 276 students and 32 instructors. Results demonstrate initial reliability and validity of the checklist and its relationship to college persistence, university belonging, intrinsic motivation, and professor-student rapport. Students and faculty differed on their perceptions of power-sharing in the classroom, suggesting that faculty attitudes are not always translating to the student experience. Implications for educational developers working to support inclusive pedagogy are provided.

title: A syllabus analysis tool to advance inclusive and equitable teaching
text_snippet: A syllabus analysis tool to advance inclusive and equitable teaching A course syllabus provides an easily accessible source of information about the learning activities, teaching methods, assessments, and policies the instructor intends to apply in a course. This paper describes our process of developing and applying a rubric designed to identify and describe inclusive and equitable practices observed in course syllabi. Using the rubric as a tool, we analyzed course syllabi as one of multiple data sources in a larger multi-method project aimed at guiding departmental change in inclusive and equitable teaching. Our approach yielded insights into teaching practices within an individual course and allowed us to observe patterns in pedagogy across courses and within and across departments. This paper also discusses outcomes from the syllabus analysis, including how we presented and discussed department-specific findings to guide changes in departmental policies and instructor pedagogy. Finally, we offer potential applications and considerations for educational developers and departmental leaders seeking to borrow and adapt this tool to analyze and share data on the inclusive and equitable teaching practices observed in course syllabi.

title: The Syllabus Challenge: A faculty development intervention for inclusive syllabus practices
text_snippet: The Syllabus Challenge: A faculty development intervention for inclusive syllabus practices Due to lack of research to track inclusive teaching behavior changes, the extent of faculty application of inclusive teaching practices remains unknown. Therefore, direct evaluation of faculty behavior change is needed to understand the process of incorporating inclusive practices into their teaching such as through the syllabus or course design. This study investigated the impact of a faculty development workshop and Syllabus Challenge toolkit using a pre-post survey of faculty attitudes toward inclusive teaching, self-efficacy, intentions to incorporate inclusive teaching, and actual inclusive changes via pre-post syllabi comparisons. Based on pre/post workshop surveys, faculty positive attitudes, inclusive teaching self-efficacy, and inclusive teaching behavioral intentions increased following the intervention. Comparisons of course syllabi revealed that faculty made between 1 and 9 inclusive syllabus changes across sections of the syllabi. title: Centering student perspectives and equity data in a multi-institutional learning community program
text_snippet: Centering student perspectives and equity data in a multi-institutional learning community program The STEM Equity Learning Community (SELC) project guided multidisciplinary teams from nine large, public research institutions through a yearlong experience. We aimed to support instructors and undergraduate students in developing equity-mindedness to drive structural change efforts on their campuses. The SELCs were supported by access to equity data, which included student enrollment and performance in courses disaggregated by student demographics. The learning communities prioritized collaborations between students and instructors that facilitated authentic interactions and cross-institutional partnerships. In this paper we investigate the value added of the SELC experience, measuring impact on participants and institutions and highlighting the power of student voice throughout the project. An analysis of pre- (N=55) and post-survey data (N=58) from program participants and reflections from project leadership reveal key nuances of the program that can inform best practices for equity-minded STEM reform.
